en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics 47.
The Training Rule for Mahānāma:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Now at that time, Mahānāma the Sakyan had an abundance of medicine.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to offer the Saṅgha an invitation to accept medicine for four months.”
“Excellent, excellent, Mahānāma!
Therefore, Mahānāma, invite the Saṅgha for four months’ supply of medicine.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not consent.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to accept an invitation for medicinal requisites for four months.
Now at that time, the monks requested a small amount of medicine from Mahānāma the Sakyan. In that way, Mahānāma the Sakyan’s supply of medicine became abundant.

A second time, Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha to partake of medicine for another four months.
“Excellent, excellent, Mahānāma!”
"In that case, Mahānāma, invite the Saṅgha for another four months' supply of medicine.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, to accept even a second invitation.
Now at that time, the monks requested only a small amount of medicine from Mahānāma the Sakyan. Consequently, Mahānāma the Sakyan’s supply of medicine remained abundant.

A third time, Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha to accept medicinal requisites for as long as I live.
“Excellent, excellent, Mahānāma!
In that case, Mahānāma, you should invite the Saṅgha to accept medicinal requisites for as long as you live.”
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the bhikkhus did not consent.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, I allow you to accept even a permanent invitation.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were poorly clad, poorly robed, and lacking in proper deportment.
Mahānāma the Sakyan was one who spoke out: “Venerable sirs, why are you poorly clad, poorly robed, and lacking in proper deportment?
Should a person gone forth not indeed be well-clad, well-robed, and endowed with proper deportment?”
The group-of-six monks became resentful toward Mahānāma the Sakyan.
Then it occurred to the group-of-six monks: "By what means might we make Mahānāma the Sakyan feel dejected? Then it occurred to the group-of-six monks:
"Friends, Mahānāma the Sakyan has invited the Saṅgha to medicaments. Come, friends, let us ask Mahānāma the Sakyan for ghee."
Then the group-of-six monks approached Mahānāma the Sakyan; having approached him, they said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan: “Friend, we have need of a doṇa of ghee.
“Venerable sirs, wait until tomorrow;
the people have gone to the cow-pen to fetch ghee.”
“You shall take it at the proper time.
A second time...
and a third time, the group-of-six monks said this to Mahānāma the Sakyan: “Friend, we have need of a doṇa of ghee.”
“Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow.
The people have gone to the cow-pen to fetch ghee;
you will receive it at the proper time.”
“But why, friend, did you not give when you were invited by one who wished to give, yet after being invited, you did not give?
Then Mahānāma the Sakyan complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying, “How can it be that the venerable ones, when told, ‘Venerable sirs, please wait until tomorrow,’ would not come?
The monks heard Mahānāma the Sakyan as he was complaining, grumbling, and becoming indignant.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six bhikkhus, when told by Mahānāma the Sakyan, ‘Venerable sirs, please wait until tomorrow,’ not come? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that you did not come when told by Mahānāma the Sakyan, ‘Venerable sirs, please wait until tomorrow’?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, when told by Mahānāma the Sakyan, ‘Venerable sirs, please wait until tomorrow,’ not come?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence… And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

‘A monk who is not ill may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation; if he should accept it beyond that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
"A sick monk may accept an invitation for requisites for four months" means he may accept an invitation for requisites on account of illness.
"He may also accept a further invitation" means...
"I will inform him when I become ill.
One may also accept a permanent invitation, thinking:
"I will inform him when I become ill."
If one should accept it beyond that:
there is an invitation limited by medicine, not limited by night;
there is an invitation limited by night, not limited by medicine.
There is an invitation ceremony limited by medicine and limited by night;
there is an invitation ceremony neither limited by medicine nor limited by night.
"Limited by medicine" means:
Medicines are delimited: “I invite [with] this many medicines.
The nights are delimited: “I invite during this many nights.”

"Having a limit of medicine and a limit of nights" means that both the medicines have been delimited and the nights have been delimited, [thinking]: "I shall invite [others] after using this much medicine for this many nights.
"Neither having a limit of medicine nor a limit of nights" means...
When medicines are not restricted and the nights are not restricted:
regarding the limit of medicines—if, having been invited with certain medicines, he requests other medicines excluding those medicines, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Regarding the limit of nights—if, having been invited during certain nights, he requests [medicines] during other nights excluding those nights, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Regarding the limit of medicine and the limit of the night: having excluded those medicines for which he has been invited [to accept],
and having excluded those nights on which he was invited, if he requests other medicines on other nights,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
There is no offense if it is not within the limit of medicine nor within the limit of the night.
If she asks for medicine when there is no need for medicine, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she asks for one kind of medicine when there is need for another kind of medicine, there is an offense of expiation.
If one asks for medicine when it exceeds that limit, perceiving it as exceeding that limit, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one asks for medicine when it exceeds that limit, being uncertain of it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one asks for medicine when it exceeds that limit, perceiving it as not exceeding that limit, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is not more than that, yet one perceives it as more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not more than that, yet one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not more than that, and one perceives it as not more than that, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he requests those very medicines with which he was invited,
or if he requests them during those very nights for which he was invited.
If, having declared, “We have been invited by you with these medicines, and we have need of this and that medicine,” she makes a request;
or if, having declared, “Those nights during which we were invited by you have passed, and we have need of medicine,” she makes a request from her relatives.
When they have been invited,
for the sake of another,
with one's own wealth.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The seventh training rule concerning Mahānāma is finished.
